claim: Mice fed a HFHSD for one day were glucose intolerant.
source: Mice fed a HFHSD for one day were glucose intolerant and the extent of glucose intolerance plateaued by 14 d (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B showing blood glucose concentrations during glucose tolerance tests.

claim: The extent of glucose intolerance plateaued by 14 days of HFHSD feeding.
source: Mice fed a HFHSD for one day were glucose intolerant and the extent of glucose intolerance plateaued by 14 d (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B showing blood glucose concentrations during glucose tolerance tests.

claim: Adipose tissue insulin resistance was observed by 5 days of HFHSD feeding.
source: Adipose tissue insulin resistance was observed by 5 d and this degree of resistance was maintained to 42 d of HFHSD feeding (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing adipose tissue 3H-2-DOG uptake during glucose tolerance tests.

claim: The degree of adipose tissue insulin resistance was maintained to 42 days of HFHSD feeding.
source: Adipose tissue insulin resistance was observed by 5 d and this degree of resistance was maintained to 42 d of HFHSD feeding (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing adipose tissue 3H-2-DOG uptake during glucose tolerance tests.

claim: Skeletal muscle exhibited a comparatively delayed onset of insulin resistance compared to adipose tissue.
source: Skeletal muscle exhibited a comparatively delayed onset of insulin resistance consistent with previous studies (Turner et al., 2013), but also reached a maximal observed insulin resistance by 14 d (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing quadriceps 3H-2-DOG uptake during glucose tolerance tests, and by citation to Turner et al., 2013.

claim: Skeletal muscle reached maximal observed insulin resistance by 14 days of HFHSD feeding.
source: Skeletal muscle exhibited a comparatively delayed onset of insulin resistance consistent with previous studies (Turner et al., 2013), but also reached a maximal observed insulin resistance by 14 d (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing quadriceps 3H-2-DOG uptake during glucose tolerance tests.

claim: Insulin resistance in in vitro models was defined by impaired HA-GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane.
source: Insulin resistance in in vitro models was defined by impaired HA-GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane (Figure 1B) and insulin-mediated 2-deoxyglucose (2DOG) uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B showing HA-GLUT4 abundance at the plasma membrane in 3T3-L1 adipocytes treated to induce insulin resistance.

claim: Insulin resistance in in vitro models was defined by impaired insulin-mediated 2-deoxyglucose uptake.
source: Insulin resistance in in vitro models was defined by impaired HA-GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane (Figure 1B) and insulin-mediated 2-deoxyglucose (2DOG) uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E showing 3H-2-DOG uptake in 3T3-L1 adipocytes treated to induce insulin resistance.

claim: Proteomic analyses of insulin-resistant adipose tissue provided quantitative data on 2981 proteins.
source: Proteomic analyses of insulin-resistant adipose tissue and 3T3-L1 adipocytes provided quantitative data on 2981 and 3494 proteins, respectively (Figure 1C–D, Supplementary file 1-tabs A, C), 98 of which were altered at both 5 and 14 d HFHSD time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, top right panel, Supplementary file 1- tab A) and 491 in ≥2 in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, left panel, Supplementary file 1-tab C).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1C-D and Supplementary file 1-tabs A, C.

claim: Proteomic analyses of insulin-resistant 3T3-L1 adipocytes provided quantitative data on 3494 proteins.
source: Proteomic analyses of insulin-resistant adipose tissue and 3T3-L1 adipocytes provided quantitative data on 2981 and 3494 proteins, respectively (Figure 1C–D, Supplementary file 1-tabs A, C), 98 of which were altered at both 5 and 14 d HFHSD time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, top right panel, Supplementary file 1- tab A) and 491 in ≥2 in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, left panel, Supplementary file 1-tab C).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1C-D and Supplementary file 1-tabs A, C.

claim: 98 proteins were altered at both 5 and 14 day HFHSD time points in adipose tissue.
source: Proteomic analyses of insulin-resistant adipose tissue and 3T3-L1 adipocytes provided quantitative data on 2981 and 3494 proteins, respectively (Figure 1C–D, Supplementary file 1-tabs A, C), 98 of which were altered at both 5 and 14 d HFHSD time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, top right panel, Supplementary file 1- tab A) and 491 in ≥2 in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, left panel, Supplementary file 1-tab C).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1-tab A.

claim: 491 proteins were altered in ≥2 in vitro models of insulin resistance.
source: Proteomic analyses of insulin-resistant adipose tissue and 3T3-L1 adipocytes provided quantitative data on 2981 and 3494 proteins, respectively (Figure 1C–D, Supplementary file 1-tabs A, C), 98 of which were altered at both 5 and 14 d HFHSD time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, top right panel, Supplementary file 1- tab A) and 491 in ≥2 in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, left panel, Supplementary file 1-tab C).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1-tab C.

claim: 19 proteins were common to both in vivo and in vitro proteomic analyses of insulin resistance.
source: A small subset of these (19) were common to both analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, bottom right panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1.L ) including the LRP1 chaperone LRPAP1, which is of interest because LRP1 regulates GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes (Jedrychowski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L, and by citation to Jedrychowski et al., 2010.

claim: LRPAP1 was among the 19 proteins common to both in vivo and in vitro proteomic analyses.
source: A small subset of these (19) were common to both analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, bottom right panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1.L ) including the LRP1 chaperone LRPAP1, which is of interest because LRP1 regulates GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes (Jedrychowski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L, and by citation to Jedrychowski et al., 2010.

claim: LRP1 regulates GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes.
source: A small subset of these (19) were common to both analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, bottom right panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1.L ) including the LRP1 chaperone LRPAP1, which is of interest because LRP1 regulates GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes (Jedrychowski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jedrychowski et al., 2010.

claim: 13 pathways were altered at both 5 and 14 day time points in adipose tissue from HFHSD mice.
source: From gene set enrichment analysis, 13 pathways were altered at both time points in adipose tissue from HFHSD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, top right panel, Supplementary file 1-tab E).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 1-tab E.

claim: There was a high degree of overlap in altered pathways across different in vitro models of insulin resistance.
source: Similarly, there was a high degree of overlap in altered pathways across different in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, left panel, Supplementary file 1-tab E).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 1-tab E.

claim: Ten pathways were overlapping between all models of insulin resistance.
source: Ten pathways were overlapping between all models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, bottom right panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1.M).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1M.

claim: Parallel analysis of gene expression in insulin resistance models revealed minimal overlap between regulated transcripts and proteins in all models.
source: Intriguingly, parallel analysis of gene expression in these models revealed minimal overlap between regulated transcripts and proteins in all models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–K, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I-K and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Of the 98 proteins altered at both 5 and 14 day HFHSD, only 12 were altered at the mRNA level.
source: For example, of the 98 proteins altered at both 5 and 14 d HFHSD only 12 were altered at the mRNA level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, Supplementary file 2-tab A), and there was limited concordance between changes in proteins and transcript expression for the 19 proteins and 10 pathways found to be altered in both in vivo and in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–M).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and Supplementary file 2-tab A.

claim: There was limited concordance between changes in proteins and transcript expression for the 19 proteins and 10 pathways found to be altered in both in vivo and in vitro models.
source: For example, of the 98 proteins altered at both 5 and 14 d HFHSD only 12 were altered at the mRNA level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, Supplementary file 2-tab A), and there was limited concordance between changes in proteins and transcript expression for the 19 proteins and 10 pathways found to be altered in both in vivo and in vitro models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–M).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and proteomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L-M.

claim: The lack of concordance between gene and protein expression emphasizes how crucial proteomic analyses are in identifying causal links to metabolic disease.
source: This lack of concordance between gene and protein expression emphasises how crucial proteomic analyses are in identifying causal links to metabolic disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed lack of concordance between gene and protein expression in the insulin resistance models.

claim: 13 KEGG pathways (excluding disease pathways) were highly altered (z-score >4) in both in vivo and in vitro analyses of insulin resistance.
source: There were 13 KEGG pathways (excluding disease pathways) that were highly altered (z-score >4) in in vivo and in vitro analyses.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data presented in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation was the most highly altered pathway in both in vivo and in vitro models of insulin resistance.
source: Oxidative phosphorylation was most highly altered in both in vivo and in vitro models, and other pathways of interest included TCA cycle, branched chain amino acid metabolism (valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation), proteasome, ribosome, spliceosome, N-glycan biosynthesis and terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 3- tab B).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data presented in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: Other pathways of interest altered in insulin resistance included TCA cycle, branched chain amino acid metabolism, proteasome, ribosome, spliceosome, N-glycan biosynthesis and terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway.
source: Oxidative phosphorylation was most highly altered in both in vivo and in vitro models, and other pathways of interest included TCA cycle, branched chain amino acid metabolism (valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation), proteasome, ribosome, spliceosome, N-glycan biosynthesis and terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 3- tab B).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data presented in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: Proteomic analysis of adipose tissue from a cohort of obese subjects quantified 4481 proteins across 22 subjects.
source: We quantified 4481 proteins across 22 subjects and correlated the expression of proteins (Supplementary file 3- tab A) and pathways (Supplementary file 3- tab B) with clinical features that are diagnostic of insulin sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Supplementary file 3-tab A.

claim: 299 proteins were positively correlated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue.
source: We identified 299 proteins (Supplementary file 3- tab A) and 26 pathways (Supplementary file 3- tab B) that were positively correlated with insulin sensitivity and 142 proteins and two pathways (ribosome, spliceosome) that were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity (r = <−0.423 or >0.423) (Supplementary file 3- tabs A, B).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data and correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3-tab A.

claim: 26 pathways were positively correlated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue.
source: We identified 299 proteins (Supplementary file 3- tab A) and 26 pathways (Supplementary file 3- tab B) that were positively correlated with insulin sensitivity and 142 proteins and two pathways (ribosome, spliceosome) that were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity (r = <−0.423 or >0.423) (Supplementary file 3- tabs A, B).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and correlation data presented in Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: 142 proteins were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue.
source: We identified 299 proteins (Supplementary file 3- tab A) and 26 pathways (Supplementary file 3- tab B) that were positively correlated with insulin sensitivity and 142 proteins and two pathways (ribosome, spliceosome) that were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity (r = <−0.423 or >0.423) (Supplementary file 3- tabs A, B).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data and correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3-tab A.

claim: Two pathways (ribosome, spliceosome) were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue.
source: We identified 299 proteins (Supplementary file 3- tab A) and 26 pathways (Supplementary file 3- tab B) that were positively correlated with insulin sensitivity and 142 proteins and two pathways (ribosome, spliceosome) that were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity (r = <−0.423 or >0.423) (Supplementary file 3- tabs A, B).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and correlation data presented in Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: The PPAR signalling pathway was positively associated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue.
source: Importantly, the PPAR signalling pathway, a known regulator of adipose insulin sensitivity (Sugii et al., 2009), was positively associated with insulin sensitivity in this analysis.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and correlation data, and by citation to Sugii et al., 2009.

claim: PPAR signalling pathway is a known regulator of adipose insulin sensitivity.
source: Importantly, the PPAR signalling pathway, a known regulator of adipose insulin sensitivity (Sugii et al., 2009), was positively associated with insulin sensitivity in this analysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sugii et al., 2009.

claim: Five pathways from the integrated proteomic analysis were positively associated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue: spliceosome, central carbon metabolism, amino acid metabolism including branched chain amino acid synthesis/degradation, and the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway.
source: Of the 13 pathways of interest from the integrated proteomic analysis of insulin resistance models (Figure 1E) only five were positively associated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 3-tab B). These comprised spliceosome, central carbon metabolism (pyruvate metabolism, TCA cycle, glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway), amino acid metabolism including branched chain amino acid synthesis/degradation and the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway, which generates precursors for isoprenoids such as cholesterol and CoQ.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and correlation data presented in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: The terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway generates precursors for isoprenoids such as cholesterol and CoQ.
source: These comprised spliceosome, central carbon metabolism (pyruvate metabolism, TCA cycle, glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway), amino acid metabolism including branched chain amino acid synthesis/degradation and the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway, which generates precursors for isoprenoids such as cholesterol and CoQ.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the mevalonate pathway.

claim: Branched chain amino acid metabolism has been implicated in adipocyte or whole body insulin sensitivity.
source: This is of interest as branched chain amino acid metabolism (Newgard et al., 2009) and spliceosome function (Vernia et al., 2016) have been implicated in adipocyte or whole body insulin sensitivity, providing support for our analysis pipeline.
evidence: Supported by citation to Newgard et al., 2009.

claim: Spliceosome function has been implicated in adipocyte or whole body insulin sensitivity.
source: This is of interest as branched chain amino acid metabolism (Newgard et al., 2009) and spliceosome function (Vernia et al., 2016) have been implicated in adipocyte or whole body insulin sensitivity, providing support for our analysis pipeline.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vernia et al., 2016.

claim: COQ7 was lower in insulin-resistant adipose tissue from humans and mice.
source: COQ7 and COQ9 were lower in insulin-resistant adipose tissue from humans and mice (Figure 2), while ADCK3/COQ8 was dysregulated at the protein and mRNA levels in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2.

claim: COQ9 was lower in insulin-resistant adipose tissue from humans and mice.
source: COQ7 and COQ9 were lower in insulin-resistant adipose tissue from humans and mice (Figure 2), while ADCK3/COQ8 was dysregulated at the protein and mRNA levels in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2.

claim: ADCK3/COQ8 was dysregulated at the protein and mRNA levels in vitro.
source: COQ7 and COQ9 were lower in insulin-resistant adipose tissue from humans and mice (Figure 2), while ADCK3/COQ8 was dysregulated at the protein and mRNA levels in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic and transcriptomic data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Integrated analysis of insulin-resistant proteomes from in vivo and in vitro models, and human, pointed toward a convergence upon dysregulated CoQ biosynthesis in insulin resistance.
source: Our integrated analysis of insulin-resistant proteomes from in vivo and in vitro models, and human, pointed toward a convergence upon dysregulated CoQ biosynthesis in insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrated proteomic analysis showing dysregulation of CoQ biosynthesis pathway components across multiple models.

claim: Whole-cell CoQ concentrations were decreased in in vitro models of insulin resistance.
source: Whole-cell CoQ concentrations were decreased in in vitro models (Figure 3A) but not in insulin-resistant adipose tissue (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Whole-cell CoQ concentrations were not decreased in insulin-resistant adipose tissue.
source: Whole-cell CoQ concentrations were decreased in in vitro models (Figure 3A) but not in insulin-resistant adipose tissue (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a selective depletion of CoQ in mitochondria across all models of insulin resistance.
source: To investigate this, we analysed CoQ in subcellular fractions from 3T3-L1 adipocytes and adipose tissue. This revealed a selective depletion of CoQ in mitochondria across all models (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data in subcellular fractions presented in Figure 3C-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The decrease in mitochondrial CoQ was not due to changes in mitochondrial content.
source: This decrease was not due to changes in mitochondrial content (assessed via citrate synthase activity and OXPHOS subunit abundance; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–J, Supplementary file 2- tabs A-D).
evidence: Supported by citrate synthase activity and OXPHOS subunit abundance data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-J and Supplementary file 2-tabs A-D.

claim: Adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 was positively correlated with insulin-induced suppression of NEFAs in obese humans.
source: Consistent with data from model systems, adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 (the major form of CoQ in humans) was positively correlated with insulin-induced suppression of NEFAs (Figure 3E–F, Table 1) and whole-body insulin sensitivity (GIR) in obese humans (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K–L, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement and correlation data presented in Figure 3E-F and Table 1.

claim: Adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 was positively correlated with whole-body insulin sensitivity (GIR) in obese humans.
source: Consistent with data from model systems, adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 (the major form of CoQ in humans) was positively correlated with insulin-induced suppression of NEFAs (Figure 3E–F, Table 1) and whole-body insulin sensitivity (GIR) in obese humans (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K–L, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement and correlation data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K-L and Table 1.

claim: Mitochondrial CoQ10 was significantly and positively correlated with expression of proteins in the CoQ biosynthesis pathway.
source: Mitochondrial CoQ10 was also significantly and positively correlated with expression of proteins in the CoQ biosynthesis pathway (r =+0.52) (Supplementary file 3-tab B) indicating that decreased biosynthesis may contribute to lower mitochondrial CoQ in insulin resistance.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data presented in Supplementary file 3-tab B.

claim: Decreased biosynthesis may contribute to lower mitochondrial CoQ in insulin resistance.
source: Mitochondrial CoQ10 was also significantly and positively correlated with expression of proteins in the CoQ biosynthesis pathway (r =+0.52) (Supplementary file 3-tab B) indicating that decreased biosynthesis may contribute to lower mitochondrial CoQ in insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive correlation between mitochondrial CoQ10 and expression of CoQ biosynthesis pathway proteins.

claim: Stratification of participants by adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 revealed no effect of age or BMI.
source: Stratification of participants by adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 revealed no effect of age or BMI (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: Decreases in mitochondrial CoQ are an obesity-independent feature of adipocyte insulin resistance.
source: These findings reveal that decreases in mitochondrial CoQ are an obesity-independent feature of adipocyte insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mitochondrial CoQ10 levels correlate with insulin sensitivity independent of BMI in the human cohort.

claim: CoQ biosynthesis rates were lower in cells treated with dexamethasone or TNF-α.
source: Consistent with pathway analysis and our intracellular measures of cholesterol content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–P), CoQ biosynthesis rates were lower in cells treated with dexamethasone or TNF-α but elevated in response to chronic insulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: Supported by CoQ biosynthesis rate data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: CoQ biosynthesis rates were elevated in response to chronic insulin.
source: Consistent with pathway analysis and our intracellular measures of cholesterol content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–P), CoQ biosynthesis rates were lower in cells treated with dexamethasone or TNF-α but elevated in response to chronic insulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: Supported by CoQ biosynthesis rate data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: Dexamethasone and TNF-α treatments lower mitochondrial CoQ largely via reduced biosynthesis.
source: Together, it appears probable that dexamethasone and TNF-α treatments lower mitochondrial CoQ largely via reduced biosynthesis, although increased CoQ in microsomal and PM subcellular fractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) in these models point to additional dysregulation of CoQ trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in CoQ biosynthesis rates and increased CoQ in other subcellular fractions in dexamethasone and TNF-α treated cells.

claim: Increased CoQ in microsomal and PM subcellular fractions in dexamethasone and TNF-α models point to additional dysregulation of CoQ trafficking.
source: Together, it appears probable that dexamethasone and TNF-α treatments lower mitochondrial CoQ largely via reduced biosynthesis, although increased CoQ in microsomal and PM subcellular fractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) in these models point to additional dysregulation of CoQ trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in CoQ in microsomal and PM subcellular fractions in dexamethasone and TNF-α treated cells.

claim: It is likely that decreased CoQ biosynthesis contributes to loss of CoQ in dexamethasone and TNF-α models since these models replicate the lower content of mevalonate/CoQ biosynthesis pathway proteins measured in mice and humans.
source: Since these models replicate the lower content of mevalonate/CoQ biosynthesis pathway proteins measured in mice and humans, it is likely that decreased CoQ biosynthesis contributes to loss of CoQ in these more physiological systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between the in vitro models and the in vivo observations in mice and humans.

claim: Additional pathway(s) likely contribute to dysregulated mitochondrial CoQ homeostasis in adipocytes treated with chronic insulin.
source: This does not appear to be the case for adipocytes treated with chronic insulin, where additional pathway(s) likely contribute to dysregulated mitochondrial CoQ homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CoQ biosynthesis rates are elevated in chronic insulin treated cells despite lower mitochondrial CoQ.

claim: Mitochondrial CoQ was decreased at 14 and 42 day HFHSD feeding in muscle.
source: In muscle, we found decreased mitochondrial CoQ at 14 and 42 d HFHSD feeding (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data in muscle mitochondria presented in Figure 3G.

claim: The time points of decreased mitochondrial CoQ in muscle correlate with the emergence of insulin resistance in muscle.
source: These time points correlate with the emergence of insulin resistance in muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between decreased mitochondrial CoQ and insulin resistance in muscle.

claim: Liver mitochondrial CoQ was unchanged in response to HFHSD feeding.
source: Liver mitochondrial CoQ was unchanged in response to HFHSD feeding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1S), despite changes in total CoQ at 5 d HFHSD feeding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1T).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data in liver mitochondria presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1S.

claim: Changes in cholesterol content in in vitro models, adipose tissue, muscle and liver were inconsistent with a causal role in insulin resistance across multiple tissues.
source: Changes in cholesterol content in in vitro models (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–P), adipose tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1U), muscle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1V) and liver (Figure 3—figure supplement 1W) were inconsistent with a causal role in insulin resistance across multiple tissues.
evidence: Supported by cholesterol measurement data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1M-W.

claim: A decrease in mitochondrial CoQ may be involved at an early stage in the development of insulin resistance in muscle and adipose tissue.
source: These data suggest that a decrease in mitochondrial CoQ may be involved at an early stage in the development of insulin resistance in muscle and adipose tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between decreased mitochondrial CoQ and the emergence of insulin resistance in muscle and adipose tissue.

claim: Addition of CoQ9 increased mitochondrial CoQ9 in insulin-resistant cells.
source: Addition of CoQ9 had no effect in control cells but increased mitochondrial CoQ9 in insulin-resistant cells (Figure 4A) and both CoQ9 and CoQ10 improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation and 2DOG uptake in all cell models (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: CoQ9 and CoQ10 improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation in all cell models of insulin resistance.
source: Addition of CoQ9 had no effect in control cells but increased mitochondrial CoQ9 in insulin-resistant cells (Figure 4A) and both CoQ9 and CoQ10 improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation and 2DOG uptake in all cell models (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by HA-GLUT4 translocation data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: CoQ9 and CoQ10 improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in all cell models of insulin resistance.
source: Addition of CoQ9 had no effect in control cells but increased mitochondrial CoQ9 in insulin-resistant cells (Figure 4A) and both CoQ9 and CoQ10 improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation and 2DOG uptake in all cell models (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by 2DOG uptake data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Dex or TNFα treatment enhanced basal lipolysis.
source: Dex or TNFα treatment enhanced basal lipolysis as previously described (Souza et al., 1998; Xu et al., 2009) and insulin-regulated inhibition of lipolysis was defective in all models (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by lipolysis data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E, and by citations to Souza et al., 1998 and Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Insulin-regulated inhibition of lipolysis was defective in all models of insulin resistance.
source: Dex or TNFα treatment enhanced basal lipolysis as previously described (Souza et al., 1998; Xu et al., 2009) and insulin-regulated inhibition of lipolysis was defective in all models (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by lipolysis data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Provision of CoQ9 increased suppression of lipolysis by insulin in in vitro models.
source: Provision of CoQ9 had no effect in control cells but increased suppression of lipolysis by insulin in in vitro models (albeit not significantly in the TNF model; p=0.11).
evidence: Supported by lipolysis data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: CoQ10 administration improved whole-body glucose tolerance in mice fed a HFHSD for 5 or 14 days.
source: CoQ10 administration improved whole-body glucose tolerance in mice fed a HFHSD for 5 or 14 d (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G) without altering insulin secretion (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data presented in Figure 4D-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: CoQ10 administration did not alter insulin secretion in mice fed a HFHSD.
source: CoQ10 administration improved whole-body glucose tolerance in mice fed a HFHSD for 5 or 14 d (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G) without altering insulin secretion (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by insulin measurement data presented in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Improved glucose tolerance with CoQ10 was accompanied by increased suppression of NEFAs during the GTT.
source: Improved glucose tolerance was accompanied by increased suppression of NEFAs (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I) and 2DOG clearance into epididymal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J) and inguinal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, p=0.06) adipose depots and quadriceps (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L, p=0.08) during the GTT.
evidence: Supported by NEFA measurement data presented in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Improved glucose tolerance with CoQ10 was accompanied by increased 2DOG clearance into epididymal adipose depots during the GTT.
source: Improved glucose tolerance was accompanied by increased suppression of NEFAs (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I) and 2DOG clearance into epididymal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J) and inguinal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, p=0.06) adipose depots and quadriceps (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L, p=0.08) during the GTT.
evidence: Supported by 2DOG uptake data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: CoQ10 increased insulin responsiveness of HFHSD-fed mice during an ITT as measured by blood glucose excursion.
source: In a more direct measure of insulin sensitivity in vivo, CoQ10 also increased insulin responsiveness of HFHSD-fed mice during an ITT as measured by blood glucose excursion (Figure 4H) and 2DOG uptake into epididymal and inguinal fat pads and quadriceps muscle (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: Supported by insulin tolerance test data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: CoQ10 increased 2DOG uptake into epididymal and inguinal fat pads and quadriceps muscle during an ITT.
source: In a more direct measure of insulin sensitivity in vivo, CoQ10 also increased insulin responsiveness of HFHSD-fed mice during an ITT as measured by blood glucose excursion (Figure 4H) and 2DOG uptake into epididymal and inguinal fat pads and quadriceps muscle (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: Supported by 2DOG uptake data presented in Figure 4I-K.

claim: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 days dose-dependently increased CoQ10 in mitochondria from epididymal adipose tissue.
source: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 d dose-dependently increased CoQ10 in mitochondria from epididymal adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), improved glucose tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N–O) and improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in an ex vivo assay using adipose tissue explants (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M.

claim: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 days improved glucose tolerance.
source: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 d dose-dependently increased CoQ10 in mitochondria from epididymal adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), improved glucose tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N–O) and improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in an ex vivo assay using adipose tissue explants (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1N-O.

claim: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 days improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in an ex vivo assay using adipose tissue explants.
source: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 d dose-dependently increased CoQ10 in mitochondria from epididymal adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), improved glucose tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N–O) and improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in an ex vivo assay using adipose tissue explants (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by 2DOG uptake data in adipose tissue explants presented in Figure 4L.

claim: CoQ10 did not alter whole body or epididymal fat pad mass.
source: CoQ10 did not alter whole body or epididymal fat pad mass (Figure 4—figure supplement 1P–Q).
evidence: Supported by body mass and fat pad mass data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1P-Q.

claim: Provision of exogenous CoQ improves insulin-regulated glucose uptake.
source: Together, these data suggest that provision of exogenous CoQ improves insulin-regulated glucose uptake and that lower CoQ content may contribute to insulin resistance in adipose tissue and muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed improvements in insulin-regulated glucose uptake with CoQ supplementation in multiple models.

claim: Lower CoQ content may contribute to insulin resistance in adipose tissue and muscle.
source: Together, these data suggest that provision of exogenous CoQ improves insulin-regulated glucose uptake and that lower CoQ content may contribute to insulin resistance in adipose tissue and muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed improvements in insulin-regulated glucose uptake with CoQ supplementation in multiple models.

claim: 4-nitrobenzoic acid (NB) and 4-cholorobenzoic acid (CB) competitively inhibit 4-hydroxybenzoate:polyprenyl transferase (Coq2).
source: To achieve this, we incubated adipocytes with 4-nitrobenzoic acid (NB) or 4-cholorobenzoic acid (CB) (Alam et al., 1975; Forsman et al., 2010) to competitively inhibit 4-hydroxybenzoate:polyprenyl transferase (Coq2) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alam et al., 1975 and Forsman et al., 2010.

claim: Both NB and CB inhibitors decreased mitochondrial CoQ9 to a similar extent to that observed in insulin-resistant adipocytes.
source: Both inhibitors decreased mitochondrial CoQ9 (Figure 5A) to a similar extent to that observed in insulin-resistant adipocytes (Figure 3C), while CoQ9 supplementation restored normal mitochondrial CoQ9 concentrations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 5A and Figure 3C.

claim: CoQ9 supplementation restored normal mitochondrial CoQ9 concentrations in cells treated with NB or CB.
source: Both inhibitors decreased mitochondrial CoQ9 (Figure 5A) to a similar extent to that observed in insulin-resistant adipocytes (Figure 3C), while CoQ9 supplementation restored normal mitochondrial CoQ9 concentrations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Both NB and CB inhibitors caused insulin resistance in adipocytes which could be reversed with provision of CoQ.
source: Importantly, both inhibitors caused insulin resistance in adipocytes (Figure 5B–5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B) which could be reversed with provision of CoQ.
evidence: Supported by insulin sensitivity data presented in Figure 5B-5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: siRNA knock down of Coq7 or Coq9 lowered mitochondrial CoQ9.
source: Similarly, siRNA knock down of the key regulatory proteins in CoQ biosynthesis that were down-regulated in insulin-resistant mouse and human adipose tissue (Coq7 or Coq9) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D) lowered mitochondrial CoQ9 (Figure 5D) and triggered insulin resistance (Figure 5E–5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: siRNA knock down of Coq7 or Coq9 triggered insulin resistance.
source: Similarly, siRNA knock down of the key regulatory proteins in CoQ biosynthesis that were down-regulated in insulin-resistant mouse and human adipose tissue (Coq7 or Coq9) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D) lowered mitochondrial CoQ9 (Figure 5D) and triggered insulin resistance (Figure 5E–5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by insulin sensitivity data presented in Figure 5E-5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Insulin resistance triggered by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis occurred independently of consistent defects in insulin signalling to Akt or TBC1D4.
source: Insulin resistance triggered by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis occurred independently of consistent defects in insulin signalling to the key regulators of glucose transport (Akt or the Akt substrate TBC1D4), or changes in GLUT4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–M).
evidence: Supported by insulin signalling data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-M.

claim: Insulin resistance triggered by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis occurred independently of changes in GLUT4 expression.
source: Insulin resistance triggered by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis occurred independently of consistent defects in insulin signalling to the key regulators of glucose transport (Akt or the Akt substrate TBC1D4), or changes in GLUT4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–M).
evidence: Supported by GLUT4 expression data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-M.

claim: CoQ provision did not alter signalling responses or GLUT4 expression in any in vitro models of insulin resistance.
source: Similarly, CoQ provision did not alter signalling responses or GLUT4 expression in any in vitro models of insulin resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N–Q) despite improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation, 2DOG uptake and suppression of lipolysis under these conditions (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by insulin signalling and GLUT4 expression data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1N-Q.

claim: Insulin resistance is not driven by overt and consistent defects in proximal insulin signalling.
source: These data are consistent with previous reports that insulin resistance is not driven by overt and consistent defects in proximal insulin signalling (Hoehn et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoehn et al., 2008 and Tan et al., 2015.

claim: Statins have recently been shown to be associated with progression to type two diabetes in humans.
source: The link between CoQ and insulin resistance is of interest in the context of statins that target the mevalonate pathway and have recently been shown to be associated with progression to type two diabetes in humans (Cederberg et al., 2015; Preiss et al., 2011; Sattar et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cederberg et al., 2015, Preiss et al., 2011, and Sattar et al., 2010.

claim: Both simvastatin and atorvastatin lowered cellular cholesterol in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Both statins lowered cellular cholesterol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1R) and CoQ content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1S), providing proof-of-principle that lower mevalonate pathway activity influences cellular CoQ content in adipocytes.
evidence: Supported by cholesterol measurement data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1R.

claim: Both simvastatin and atorvastatin lowered CoQ content in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Both statins lowered cellular cholesterol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1R) and CoQ content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1S), providing proof-of-principle that lower mevalonate pathway activity influences cellular CoQ content in adipocytes.
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1S.

claim: Lower mevalonate pathway activity influences cellular CoQ content in adipocytes.
source: Both statins lowered cellular cholesterol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1R) and CoQ content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1S), providing proof-of-principle that lower mevalonate pathway activity influences cellular CoQ content in adipocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that statins, which inhibit the mevalonate pathway, lower CoQ content in adipocytes.

claim: Statins induced insulin resistance in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Statins induced insulin resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1T), and this was reversed by providing CoQ9 or mevalonate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1T).
evidence: Supported by insulin sensitivity data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1T.

claim: Statin-induced insulin resistance was reversed by providing CoQ9 or mevalonate.
source: Statins induced insulin resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1T), and this was reversed by providing CoQ9 or mevalonate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1T).
evidence: Supported by insulin sensitivity data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1T.

claim: Loss of CoQ is sufficient to induce adipocyte insulin resistance.
source: Together with the observation that more specific inhibitors of the CoQ biosynthetic pathway also trigger insulin resistance, these data provide convincing evidence that loss of CoQ is sufficient to induce adipocyte insulin resistance, and this may contribute to off-target effects of statin therapy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple methods of lowering CoQ (pharmacological inhibition, genetic knockdown, statins) all induce insulin resistance.

claim: Loss of CoQ may contribute to off-target effects of statin therapy.
source: Together with the observation that more specific inhibitors of the CoQ biosynthetic pathway also trigger insulin resistance, these data provide convincing evidence that loss of CoQ is sufficient to induce adipocyte insulin resistance, and this may contribute to off-target effects of statin therapy.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that statins lower CoQ and induce insulin resistance in adipocytes.

claim: Mitochondrial CoQ is essential for cellular respiration, as it shuttles electrons from various membrane-bound/associated dehydrogenase complexes to complex III during oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Mitochondrial CoQ is essential for cellular respiration, as it shuttles electrons from various membrane-bound/associated dehydrogenase complexes to complex III during oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the role of CoQ in mitochondrial respiration.

claim: CoQ can regulate the formation of superoxide anion radicals from the various CoQ-interacting sites of complexes I, II and III.
source: In addition, CoQ can regulate the formation of superoxide anion radicals from the various CoQ-interacting sites of complexes I, II and III.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the role of CoQ in regulating superoxide production.

claim: Excess mitochondrial CoQ above that required for maximal respiratory flux can be thought of as an 'electron sink'.
source: In this respect, excess mitochondrial CoQ above that required for maximal respiratory flux can be thought of as an 'electron sink'.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the role of CoQ in mitochondrial electron transport.

claim: Previous studies have shown that modest loss of mitochondrial CoQ can be tolerated for electron transport activity, but at the cost of increased mitochondrial oxidants.
source: Consistent with this concept, previous studies have shown that modest loss of mitochondrial CoQ can be tolerated for electron transport activity, but at the cost of increased mitochondrial oxidants (Quinzii et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quinzii et al., 2008.

claim: There was no change in the total content of PRDX1-3 in insulin-resistant models.
source: There was no change in the total content of PRDX1-3 in insulin-resistant models (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C,J) and the dimer:monomer ratio of cytosolic PRDX1 and PRDX2 also remained unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by PRDX expression data presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C, J.

claim: The dimer:monomer ratio of cytosolic PRDX1 and PRDX2 remained unchanged in insulin-resistant models.
source: There was no change in the total content of PRDX1-3 in insulin-resistant models (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C,J) and the dimer:monomer ratio of cytosolic PRDX1 and PRDX2 also remained unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by PRDX dimerization data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The dimer:monomer ratio of mitochondrial PRDX3 increased significantly in all in vitro models of insulin resistance.
source: In contrast, the dimer:monomer ratio of mitochondrial PRDX3 increased significantly in all in vitro models (Figure 6A–6B).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6A-6B.

claim: Increased dimerisation of PRDX3 was observed under conditions of pharmacological inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis.
source: Increased dimerisation of PRDX3 was also observed under conditions of pharmacological (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) or genetic inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H) of CoQ biosynthesis, with limited or no changes in PRDX2 redox state (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,I).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Increased dimerisation of PRDX3 was observed under conditions of genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis.
source: Increased dimerisation of PRDX3 was also observed under conditions of pharmacological (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) or genetic inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H) of CoQ biosynthesis, with limited or no changes in PRDX2 redox state (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,I).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Restoration of normal mitochondrial CoQ9 content by provision of exogenous CoQ9 lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio.
source: Restoration of normal mitochondrial CoQ9 content by provision of exogenous CoQ9 lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio (Figure 6D–6E).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6D-6E.

claim: PRDX3 dimerisation was enhanced in insulin-resistant adipose tissue at 5 and 14 day HFHSD feeding.
source: PRDX3 dimerisation was also enhanced in insulin-resistant adipose tissue at 5 and 14 d HFHSD feeding (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: In vivo administration of CoQ10 under conditions that improved insulin sensitivity lowered the PRDX3 dimer-to-monomer ratio in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In vivo administration of CoQ10 under conditions that improved insulin sensitivity lowered the PRDX3 dimer-to-monomer ratio in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Decreased mitochondrial CoQ is upstream of increased mitochondrial oxidants, most likely in the form of H2O2 in adipocyte insulin resistance.
source: Together, these data place decreased mitochondrial CoQ upstream of increased mitochondrial oxidants, most likely in the form of H2O2 in adipocyte insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in PRDX3 dimerization (a marker of H2O2) in response to decreased mitochondrial CoQ.

claim: Basal oxygen consumption was increased in multiple models of insulin resistance in 3T3-L1 adipocytes cultured in galactose.
source: In control and insulin-resistant 3T3-L1 adipocytes cultured in galactose, to force ATP-production via mitochondria (Aguer et al., 2011), we observed no defect in basal or maximal (uncoupler-induced) respiration (Figure 7A). Instead, basal oxygen consumption was increased in multiple models (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: FAD-linked respiratory capacity assessed via succinate was the only activity compromised in all models of insulin resistance in digitonin-permeabilised 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: To explore this further, we measured oxygen consumption in digitonin-permeabilised 3T3-L1 adipocytes to assess maximal respiratory function (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). In these experiments, FAD-linked respiratory capacity assessed via succinate was the only activity compromised in all models (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data in permeabilized cells presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The defect in FAD-linked respiratory capacity was specific to succinate dehydrogenase, since oxidation of medium-chain fatty acid was not altered.
source: This defect was specific to succinate dehydrogenase, since oxidation of medium-chain fatty acid (i.e., octanoylcarnitine, which also donates electrons to CoQ via electron-transferring-flavoprotein dehydrogenase [Ruzicka and Beinert, 1977]), was not altered (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and by citation to Ruzicka and Beinert, 1977.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial CoQ decreases succinate-driven complex II capacity, but this does not limit overall mitochondrial respiration in cells.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that loss of mitochondrial CoQ decreases succinate-driven complex II capacity, but this does not limit overall mitochondrial respiration in cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in complex II activity without a decrease in overall mitochondrial respiration.

claim: Mitochondrial superoxide was increased in the chronic insulin model of insulin resistance.
source: To test this directly, we determined superoxide in specific in vitro models of adipocyte insulin resistance, using LC-MS to quantify the conversion of mito-hydroethidine to the superoxide-specific product mito-2-hydroxyethidium (Zielonka et al., 2008). Mitochondrial superoxide was increased in the CI model (Figure 7E) and in adipocytes where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited (Figure 7E–7F), implying that increased mitochondrial H2O2 following loss of CoQ was due to increased superoxide production.
evidence: Supported by superoxide measurement data presented in Figure 7E, and by citation to Zielonka et al., 2008.

claim: Mitochondrial superoxide was increased in adipocytes where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited.
source: To test this directly, we determined superoxide in specific in vitro models of adipocyte insulin resistance, using LC-MS to quantify the conversion of mito-hydroethidine to the superoxide-specific product mito-2-hydroxyethidium (Zielonka et al., 2008). Mitochondrial superoxide was increased in the CI model (Figure 7E) and in adipocytes where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited (Figure 7E–7F), implying that increased mitochondrial H2O2 following loss of CoQ was due to increased superoxide production.
evidence: Supported by superoxide measurement data presented in Figure 7E-7F, and by citation to Zielonka et al., 2008.

claim: Increased mitochondrial H2O2 following loss of CoQ was due to increased superoxide production.
source: To test this directly, we determined superoxide in specific in vitro models of adipocyte insulin resistance, using LC-MS to quantify the conversion of mito-hydroethidine to the superoxide-specific product mito-2-hydroxyethidium (Zielonka et al., 2008). Mitochondrial superoxide was increased in the CI model (Figure 7E) and in adipocytes where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited (Figure 7E–7F), implying that increased mitochondrial H2O2 following loss of CoQ was due to increased superoxide production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in superoxide in models with increased H2O2.

claim: BAM15 and FCCP lowered the PRDX3 dimer/monomer status to control levels in cells treated with NB.
source: BAM15 and FCCP had no effect on PRDX3 dimerisation in control cells but lowered the PRDX3 dimer/monomer status to control levels in cells treated with NB (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), or in cells in which the expression of Coq7 and Coq9 were reduced using siRNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of CoQ increased H2O2 in a coupled respiration-dependent manner.
source: This established that loss of CoQ increased H2O2 in a coupled respiration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that uncouplers (BAM15 and FCCP) lowered PRDX3 dimerization in cells with decreased CoQ.

claim: Administration of the complex II inhibitors TTFA and malonate lowered the PRDX3 dimer/monomer ratio to near control values in cells treated to inhibit CoQ biosynthesis.
source: Administration of the complex II inhibitors TTFA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and malonate lowered the PRDX3 dimer/monomer ratio to near control values in cells treated to inhibit CoQ biosynthesis (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E) and in other models of insulin resistance (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–I), suggesting that increased H2O2 in insulin-resistant adipocytes was dependent on complex II.
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Increased H2O2 in insulin-resistant adipocytes was dependent on complex II.
source: Administration of the complex II inhibitors TTFA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and malonate lowered the PRDX3 dimer/monomer ratio to near control values in cells treated to inhibit CoQ biosynthesis (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E) and in other models of insulin resistance (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–I), suggesting that increased H2O2 in insulin-resistant adipocytes was dependent on complex II.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that complex II inhibitors lowered PRDX3 dimerization in insulin-resistant adipocytes.

claim: Rotenone had no effect on the PRDX3 redox state in NB-treated cells.
source: Rotenone had no effect on the PRDX3 redox state in NB-treated cells, similar to what was observed for antimycin A (a complex III inhibitor) and oligomycin (a complex V inhibitor) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Treatment of 3T3-L1 adipocytes with NB did not change the CoQ redox state.
source: Further, treatment of 3T3-L1 adipocytes with NB did not change the CoQ redox state, just as the CoQ redox state was not altered in other in vitro models of insulin resistance (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by CoQ redox state data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Reverse electron transport was not involved in the observed increase in superoxide/H2O2 resulting from loss of mitochondrial CoQ.
source: Since a more reduced CoQ pool is required for reverse election transport from CoQH2 to complex I (Murphy, 2009), these data suggest that reverse electron transport was not involved in the observed increase in superoxide/H2O2 resulting from loss of mitochondrial CoQ, and that complex II itself was the likely origin the oxidants (Quinlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rotenone had no effect on PRDX3 dimerization and the CoQ redox state was not altered, and supported by citations to Murphy, 2009 and Quinlan et al., 2012.

claim: Complex II itself was the likely origin of the oxidants in insulin-resistant adipocytes.
source: Since a more reduced CoQ pool is required for reverse election transport from CoQH2 to complex I (Murphy, 2009), these data suggest that reverse electron transport was not involved in the observed increase in superoxide/H2O2 resulting from loss of mitochondrial CoQ, and that complex II itself was the likely origin the oxidants (Quinlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that complex II inhibitors lowered PRDX3 dimerization and reverse electron transport was ruled out, and supported by citation to Quinlan et al., 2012.

claim: Treatment of control 3T3-L1 adipocytes with TTFA did not impair insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation.
source: Treatment of control 3T3-L1 adipocytes with TTFA did not impair insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation (Figure 7I) or insulin-regulated inhibition of lipolysis (data not shown), suggesting that impaired complex II activity does not cause adipocyte insulin resistance per se.
evidence: Supported by HA-GLUT4 translocation data presented in Figure 7I.

claim: Impaired complex II activity does not cause adipocyte insulin resistance per se.
source: Treatment of control 3T3-L1 adipocytes with TTFA did not impair insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation (Figure 7I) or insulin-regulated inhibition of lipolysis (data not shown), suggesting that impaired complex II activity does not cause adipocyte insulin resistance per se.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TTFA did not impair insulin action in control cells.

claim: Both TTFA and malonate improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation to the PM in all models of insulin resistance tested.
source: Both TTFA and malonate improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation to the PM in all models of insulin resistance tested (Figure 7I–7J), albeit not to the same level as observed in control cells.
evidence: Supported by HA-GLUT4 translocation data presented in Figure 7I-7J.

claim: TTFA improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in adipose explants isolated from mice fed a HFHSD.
source: Further, TTFA improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in adipose explants isolated from mice fed a HFHSD (Figure 7K).
evidence: Supported by 2DOG uptake data in adipose explants presented in Figure 7K.

claim: Lower mitochondrial CoQ accelerates superoxide generation, most likely from complex II, which in turn elevates the mitochondrial H2O2 burden, promotes PRDX3 dimerisation and drives insulin resistance.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that lower mitochondrial CoQ accelerates superoxide generation, most likely from complex II, which in turn elevates the mitochondrial H2O2 burden, promotes PRDX3 dimerisation and drives insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective data showing that decreased mitochondrial CoQ leads to increased superoxide from complex II, increased PRDX3 dimerization, and insulin resistance.

claim: Mitochondrial oxidants have been reported to play an important role in the development of insulin resistance in adipose and muscle tissue.
source: Mitochondrial oxidants have been reported to play an important role in the development of insulin resistance in adipose (Hoehn et al., 2009; Houstis et al., 2006; Paglialunga et al., 2015) and muscle tissue (Anderson et al., 2009; Hoehn et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoehn et al., 2009, Houstis et al., 2006, Paglialunga et al., 2015, and Anderson et al., 2009.

claim: Increased production of superoxide or H2O2 in mitochondria is thought to be the primary mechanism by which mitochondrial oxidants contribute to insulin resistance.
source: This is thought to occur primarily via increased production of superoxide or H2O2 in mitochondria (Anderson et al., 2009; Hoehn et al., 2009; Paglialunga et al., 2015), yet the proximal mechanism that triggers mitochondrial oxidant production has remained elusive.
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2009, Hoehn et al., 2009, and Paglialunga et al., 2015.

claim: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomic analysis of adipose tissue from mice fed a HFHSD, insulin-resistant 3T3-L1 adipocytes and adipose tissue from insulin-resistant humans revealed down-regulation of the mevalonate/CoQ biosynthesis pathway in multiple models.
source: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomic analysis of adipose tissue from mice fed a HFHSD, insulin-resistant 3T3-L1 adipocytes and adipose tissue from insulin-resistant humans, revealed down-regulation of the mevalonate/CoQ biosynthesis pathway in multiple models, and a separate targeted metabolite analysis revealed a common decrease in mitochondrial CoQ content in these models as well as in insulin-resistant muscle.
evidence: Supported by proteomic data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A targeted metabolite analysis revealed a common decrease in mitochondrial CoQ content in insulin-resistant adipose tissue, 3T3-L1 adipocytes, and muscle.
source: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomic analysis of adipose tissue from mice fed a HFHSD, insulin-resistant 3T3-L1 adipocytes and adipose tissue from insulin-resistant humans, revealed down-regulation of the mevalonate/CoQ biosynthesis pathway in multiple models, and a separate targeted metabolite analysis revealed a common decrease in mitochondrial CoQ content in these models as well as in insulin-resistant muscle.
evidence: Supported by CoQ measurement data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Decreased mitochondrial CoQ was sufficient to cause insulin resistance via a mechanism requiring mitochondrial oxidants.
source: Decreased mitochondrial CoQ was sufficient to cause insulin resistance via a mechanism requiring mitochondrial oxidants, while restoration of mitochondrial CoQ restored insulin sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by data showing that inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis causes insulin resistance and that this is reversed by CoQ supplementation or by scavenging mitochondrial oxidants.

claim: Restoration of mitochondrial CoQ restored insulin sensitivity.
source: Decreased mitochondrial CoQ was sufficient to cause insulin resistance via a mechanism requiring mitochondrial oxidants, while restoration of mitochondrial CoQ restored insulin sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by data showing that CoQ supplementation improves insulin sensitivity in multiple models.

claim: The pathway involves decreased expression of mevalonate pathway/CoQ biosynthetic enzymes, lower mitochondrial CoQ and insulin resistance as a result of oxidant production primarily from complex II.
source: The pathway involves decreased expression of mevalonate pathway/CoQ biosynthetic enzymes, lower mitochondrial CoQ and insulin resistance as a result of oxidant production primarily from complex II.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Many insults implicated in insulin resistance including hyperinsulinaemia, inflammation, corticosteroids and caloric excess converge upon loss of mitochondrial CoQ as a potential cause of insulin resistance.
source: Based on the current study, many insults implicated in insulin resistance including hyperinsulinaemia, inflammation, corticosteroids and caloric excess converge upon loss of mitochondrial CoQ as a potential cause of insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple different models of insulin resistance all exhibit decreased mitochondrial CoQ.

claim: Decreased expression of CoQ biosynthetic enzymes and lower CoQ synthesis rates could explain the convergence of multiple insults upon loss of mitochondrial CoQ.
source: Mechanistically, this could be explained by decreased expression of CoQ biosynthetic enzymes, and lower CoQ synthesis rates, in a majority of models studied.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in CoQ biosynthetic enzyme expression and CoQ synthesis rates in multiple models.

claim: The finding that mevalonate pathway inhibiting statins lowered CoQ content and caused insulin resistance in a CoQ-dependent manner may shed new light on the link between statin therapy in humans and insulin resistance.
source: Related to this, our finding that mevalonate pathway inhibiting statins lowered CoQ content and caused insulin resistance in a CoQ-dependent manner may shed new light on the link between statin therapy in humans and insulin resistance (Cederberg et al., 2015; Preiss et al., 2011; Sattar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that statins lower CoQ and cause insulin resistance in adipocytes, and supported by citations to Cederberg et al., 2015, Preiss et al., 2011, and Sattar et al., 2010.

claim: The lack of concordance between transcript and protein expression within the mevalonate/CoQ pathway across the different insulin-resistant models suggests that there may be multiple mechanisms by which this pathway is targeted in response to different upstream insults.
source: The lack of concordance between transcript and protein expression within the mevalonate/CoQ pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) across the different insulin-resistant models suggests that there may be multiple mechanisms by which this pathway is targeted in response to different upstream insults and this maybe mediated via either transcriptional or post-translational regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed lack of concordance between transcript and protein expression in the mevalonate/CoQ pathway.

claim: Subcellular analysis of CoQ content and data from the chronic insulin model indicate that other aspects of CoQ biology that we do not yet understand may be involved in regulating mitochondrial CoQ abundance in insulin-resistant conditions.
source: Furthermore, our subcellular analysis of CoQ content and data from the chronic insulin model indicate that other aspects of CoQ biology that we do not yet understand may be involved in regulating mitochondrial CoQ abundance in insulin-resistant conditions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that CoQ biosynthesis rates are elevated in chronic insulin treated cells despite lower mitochondrial CoQ.

claim: Various insults act in different ways, all decreasing mitochondrial CoQ as a common means of inducing insulin resistance.
source: Together, this supports the notion that various insults act in different ways, all decreasing mitochondrial CoQ as a common means of inducing insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple different insults all lead to decreased mitochondrial CoQ and insulin resistance.

claim: Modest loss of CoQ has been reported to increase mitochondrial oxidants in a range of cellular systems.
source: Modest loss of CoQ has been reported to increase mitochondrial oxidants in a range of cellular systems (Cornelius et al., 2013; Duberley et al., 2013; Quinzii et al., 2013; Quinzii et al., 2012; Rodríguez-Hernández et al., 2009), although the precise mechanism for this effect remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cornelius et al., 2013, Duberley et al., 2013, Quinzii et al., 2013, Quinzii et al., 2012, and Rodríguez-Hernández et al., 2009.

claim: Increased superoxide production from the IIF site is due to increased steady-state concentrations of the flavin radical as a result of impaired electron transfer to CoQ at the binding site IIQ, due to decreased CoQ.
source: Therefore, we hypothesise that increased superoxide production from the IIF site is due to increased steady-state concentrations of the flavin radical as a result of impaired electron transfer to CoQ at the binding site IIQ, due to decreased CoQ.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed increase in superoxide from complex II and the decrease in complex II activity.

claim: The interpretation that increased superoxide production from the IIF site is due to increased steady-state concentrations of the flavin radical is supported by the finding that maximal complex II activity was impaired in all models studied.
source: This interpretation is supported by our finding that maximal complex II activity was impaired in all models studied.
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data showing impaired complex II activity.

claim: Lower CoQ may favour reverse electron transfer to complex II, and superoxide production from IIF, under conditions where other enzymes are feeding electrons into the CoQ pool.
source: Alternatively, lower CoQ may favour reverse electron transfer to complex II, and superoxide production from IIF, under conditions where other enzymes (e.g. mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase [Orr et al., 2012]) are feeding electrons into the CoQ pool (Quinlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism, supported by citations to Orr et al., 2012 and Quinlan et al., 2012.

claim: There are likely additional sites of superoxide production since inhibition of complex II only partially rescued PRDX3 dimerisation.
source: However, there are likely additional sites of superoxide production since inhibition of complex II only partially rescued PRDX3 dimerisation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that complex II inhibitors only partially rescued PRDX3 dimerization.

claim: Improvements in insulin-stimulated glucose transport and inhibition of lipolysis with CoQ supplementation were not associated with improved insulin signalling to Akt or its downstream substrate TBC1D4.
source: Our data from cells supplemented with CoQ revealed that improvements in insulin-stimulated glucose transport and inhibition of lipolysis were not associated with improved insulin signalling to Akt or its downstream substrate TBC1D4.
evidence: Supported by insulin signalling data showing no improvement in Akt or TBC1D4 phosphorylation with CoQ supplementation.

claim: Defects in insulin-stimulated glucose transport in insulin resistance are not due to obvious defects in proximal insulin signalling.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that defects in insulin-stimulated glucose transport in insulin resistance are not due to obvious defects in proximal insulin signalling (Hoehn et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoehn et al., 2008 and Tan et al., 2015.

claim: It seems unlikely that mitochondrial oxidant-induced insulin resistance requires changes in transcription because induction of mitochondrial oxidants acutely impairs insulin action.
source: Although retrograde signalling from the mitochondria to the nucleus is well described it seems unlikely that this mitochondrial oxidant-induced insulin resistance requires changes in transcription because induction of mitochondrial oxidants acutely impairs insulin action (Hoehn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mitochondrial oxidants acutely impair insulin action, supported by citation to Hoehn et al., 2009.

claim: It is more likely that there is a presently undiscovered signal transduction pathway that communicates directly to mediators of insulin action in the cytoplasm.
source: Thus, it is more likely that there is a presently undiscovered signal transduction pathway that communicates directly to mediators of insulin action in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Serum and tissue CoQ10 concentrations are decreased in individuals with diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
source: Coenzyme Q has received considerable attention as a supplement to ameliorate a range of medical conditions, including diabetes and cardiovascular disease, based on the observation that serum and tissue CoQ10 concentrations are decreased in individuals with these conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CoQ10 levels in disease.

claim: There are reports of CoQ supplementation benefitting diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
source: While there are reports of CoQ supplementation benefitting these conditions (Amin et al., 2014; Ayer et al., 2015; Hodgson et al., 2002; Mortensen et al., 2014; Raygan et al., 2016), the efficacy of CoQ10 in the treatment of diabetes and cardiovascular diseases remains unclear (Ayer et al., 2015; Eriksson et al., 1999; Suksomboon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amin et al., 2014, Ayer et al., 2015, Hodgson et al., 2002, Mortensen et al., 2014, and Raygan et al., 2016.

claim: The efficacy of CoQ10 in the treatment of diabetes and cardiovascular diseases remains unclear.
source: While there are reports of CoQ supplementation benefitting these conditions (Amin et al., 2014; Ayer et al., 2015; Hodgson et al., 2002; Mortensen et al., 2014; Raygan et al., 2016), the efficacy of CoQ10 in the treatment of diabetes and cardiovascular diseases remains unclear (Ayer et al., 2015; Eriksson et al., 1999; Suksomboon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ayer et al., 2015, Eriksson et al., 1999, and Suksomboon et al., 2015.

claim: This study provides a reasonable rationale for targeting the CoQ biosynthesis pathway as a potential therapeutic target.
source: Our study provides a reasonable rationale for targeting the CoQ biosynthesis pathway as a potential therapeutic target.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study showing that decreased mitochondrial CoQ causes insulin resistance.

claim: Overall low bioavailability of orally administered CoQ10 or CoQ10H2 represents a substantial limitation.
source: Overall low bioavailability of orally administered CoQ10 or CoQ10H2 represents a substantial limitation, particularly in situations of modest CoQ deficiency such as those shown here to be sufficient to initiate insulin resistance, and where mitochondrial CoQ homeostasis needs to be restored in metabolic tissues such as adipose and muscle (Zhang et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 1995.

claim: Intra-peritoneal administration of CoQ to mice provided proof-of-principle that restoration of mitochondrial CoQ improves insulin action and whole body glucose tolerance.
source: We overcame this limitation in mice by intra-peritoneal administration of CoQ to provide proof-of-principle that restoration of mitochondrial CoQ improves insulin action and whole body glucose tolerance (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4 showing improved insulin action and glucose tolerance with CoQ10 administration.

claim: Intra-peritoneal administration of CoQ10 is not likely a practical strategy for the treatment of insulin resistance in humans.
source: Unfortunately, intra-peritoneal administration of CoQ10 is not likely a practical strategy for the treatment of insulin resistance in humans.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practicality of intraperitoneal administration in humans.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of the CoQ biosynthesis pathway may represent potential options for treating insulin resistance in the future.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of the CoQ biosynthesis pathway, e.g., by polyisoprenoid epoxides (Bentinger et al., 2008), or targeting additional processes that contribute to the regulation of mitochondrial CoQ content may represent potential options in the future.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic strategies, supported by citation to Bentinger et al., 2008.
