claim: The protein levels, but not the corresponding levels of the mRNAs, of the CoQ biosynthetic enzymes COQ7 and COQ9 were decreased in insulin resistance.
source: In the present study, we found that the protein levels, but not the corresponding levels of the mRNAs, of the CoQ biosynthetic enzymes COQ7 and COQ9 were decreased in insulin resistance.
evidence: Supported by proteomic and transcriptomic data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: COQ7 and COQ9 form a dimeric complex.
source: These proteins form a dimeric complex (Lohman et al., 2014) the formation of which may be regulated via a post-translational mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lohman et al., 2014.

claim: The CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilised by the atypical kinase ADCK3/COQ8.
source: Although little is known about the molecular regulation of COQ protein turnover, the CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilised by the atypical kinase ADCK3/COQ8 (He et al., 2014; Stefely et al., 2016)), mitochondrial proteases (Veling et al., 2017) and CoQ itself (He et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to He et al., 2014 and Stefely et al., 2016.

claim: The CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilised by mitochondrial proteases.
source: Although little is known about the molecular regulation of COQ protein turnover, the CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilised by the atypical kinase ADCK3/COQ8 (He et al., 2014; Stefely et al., 2016)), mitochondrial proteases (Veling et al., 2017) and CoQ itself (He et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veling et al., 2017.

claim: The CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilised by CoQ itself.
source: Although little is known about the molecular regulation of COQ protein turnover, the CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilised by the atypical kinase ADCK3/COQ8 (He et al., 2014; Stefely et al., 2016)), mitochondrial proteases (Veling et al., 2017) and CoQ itself (He et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to He et al., 2014.

claim: Destabilisation of the CoQ biosynthetic protein complex lowers expression of many of the COQ proteins altered in insulin-resistant adipose tissue, including COQ3, 7 and 9.
source: Destabilisation of the complex lowers expression of many of the COQ proteins altered in insulin-resistant adipose tissue, including COQ3, 7 and 9.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequences of destabilizing the CoQ biosynthetic protein complex.

claim: Loss of COQ7 and 9 in insulin resistance may be a result of increased turnover due to complex instability.
source: Therefore, it may be that loss of COQ7 and 9 in insulin resistance is a result of increased turnover due to complex instability.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known mechanisms of COQ protein complex regulation.

claim: Recent chemical screens have successfully identified compounds that prevent superoxide production from complex I.
source: Recent chemical screens have successfully identified compounds that prevent superoxide production from complex I (Brand et al., 2016) and III (Orr et al., 2015), without impairing electron transport.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brand et al., 2016.

claim: Recent chemical screens have successfully identified compounds that prevent superoxide production from complex III.
source: Recent chemical screens have successfully identified compounds that prevent superoxide production from complex I (Brand et al., 2016) and III (Orr et al., 2015), without impairing electron transport.
evidence: Supported by citation to Orr et al., 2015.

claim: Identifying compounds for complex II that prevent superoxide production without impairing electron transport may be useful in mitigating superoxide/H2O2 production and overcoming insulin resistance.
source: Identifying similar compounds for complex II may be useful in mitigating superoxide/H2O2 production and overcoming insulin resistance.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential therapeutic strategy.

claim: Over-expression of mitochondria-targeted catalase lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio in cells where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited.
source: This lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio in cells where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited (Figure 6H Figure 6—figure supplement 1M–O), and improved insulin responses in these conditions (Figure 6I–6J), consistent with loss of mitochondrial CoQ causing insulin resistance via mitochondrial H2O2.
evidence: Supported by PRDX3 dimerization data presented in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1M-O.

claim: Over-expression of mitochondria-targeted catalase improved insulin responses in cells where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited.
source: This lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio in cells where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited (Figure 6H Figure 6—figure supplement 1M–O), and improved insulin responses in these conditions (Figure 6I–6J), consistent with loss of mitochondrial CoQ causing insulin resistance via mitochondrial H2O2.
evidence: Supported by insulin sensitivity data presented in Figure 6I-6J.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial CoQ causes insulin resistance via mitochondrial H2O2.
source: This lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio in cells where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited (Figure 6H Figure 6—figure supplement 1M–O), and improved insulin responses in these conditions (Figure 6I–6J), consistent with loss of mitochondrial CoQ causing insulin resistance via mitochondrial H2O2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that scavenging mitochondrial H2O2 with catalase improves insulin sensitivity in cells with decreased CoQ.
